Full title: FEVER: a Large-scale Dataset for Fact Extraction and VERification
Authors: James Thorne; Andreas Vlachos; Christos Christodoulopoulos; Arpit Mittal
Research problem: Verify natural-language claims against retrieved textual evidence.
Methodology: Wikipedia sentence retrieval, evidence selection, and three-way supported/refuted/not-enough-information classification.
Dataset: FEVER: 185,445 claims derived from Wikipedia; sentence evidence annotations.
Main contribution: Introduces FEVER, a large benchmark that pairs claim verdicts with sentence-level evidence retrieval and selection.
Reported findings / publication output: Introduced a large benchmark evaluating both verdict and evidence; original pipeline remained difficult when required evidence was unavailable.
Documented limitation or task boundary c: Not established in this abstract-first pass. Current statement is an analyst inference about task/data transfer, not an author-attributed limitation; full-text review is pending.
Analyst interpretation and potential gap: Wikipedia claims do not model scientific populations, methods, measures, or uncertainty. Potential gap: Transfer to scientific drafts needs domain and scope-aware evaluation; FEVER alone cannot validate scientific alignment.
Relevance to SCOPE: Foundational retrieval-plus-inference baseline and evidence traceability framing.
Verification status: Publisher/proceedings metadata and abstract checked; full-text methods and limitations not fully reviewed. Bibliographic verification is not exhaustive critical appraisal.

Full title: Fact or Fiction: Verifying Scientific Claims
Authors: David Wadden; Shanchuan Lin; Kyle Lo; Lucy Lu Wang; Madeleine van Zuylen; Arman Cohan; Hannaneh Hajishirzi
Research problem: Retrieve scientific abstracts and identify evidence supporting or refuting claims.
Methodology: Scientific verification pipeline with abstract retrieval, rationale identification, and stance classification.
Dataset: SciFact: 1,409 expert-written claims, research abstracts, labels, rationales.
Main contribution: Defines scientific claim verification as abstract retrieval, rationale identification, and support/refute prediction; releases SciFact.
Reported findings / publication output: Established a scientific-claim benchmark; reports domain adaptation improves scientific verification over general fact-checking models.
Documented limitation or task boundary c: Paper full text checked: SciFact is explicitly framed as claim–abstract pair verification, with abstracts selected because they often contain evidence and full-text annotation was less reliable in the authors’ pilot; the authors note this bounds evidence coverage. See paper task/data design and annotation discussion.
Analyst interpretation and potential gap: Abstract-level benchmark and support/refute labels do not operationalize every study-scope dimension or reviewer workflow. Potential gap: Evaluate dimension-wise annotation and scoped relations on evidence; distinguish prototype from a new verification paradigm.
Relevance to SCOPE: Closest benchmark and core prior art for SCOPE.
Verification status: Publisher metadata, abstract, and selected full-text sections checked; interpretation boundary labeled. Bibliographic verification is not exhaustive critical appraisal.

Full title: SciFact-Open: Towards open-domain scientific claim verification
Authors: David Wadden; Kyle Lo; Bailey Kuehl; Arman Cohan; Iz Beltagy; Lucy Lu Wang; Hannaneh Hajishirzi
Research problem: Evaluate verification against a large scientific corpus with realistic retrieval difficulty.
Methodology: Pool and annotate candidate evidence from four existing verifiers; evaluate open-corpus retrieval and verification.
Dataset: SciFact-Open; 500,000 research abstracts and pooled evidence.
Main contribution: Extends scientific verification to a 500K-abstract open-corpus setting using pooled evidence annotations.
Reported findings / publication output: Systems trained on smaller corpora lost at least 15 F1; some evidence supports only a special case of a claim.
Documented limitation or task boundary c: Author-stated design constraint: exhaustive evidence annotation over a 500K-abstract corpus is infeasible; the test collection pools top predictions from four systems. Coverage is therefore pooled, not exhaustive. See paper abstract and dataset construction (Sec. 3); [ACL paper](https://aclanthology.org/2022.findings-emnlp.347/).
Analyst interpretation and potential gap: Pooling cannot ensure exhaustive evidence labels; abstracts omit methods, results, and tables. Potential gap: Study an interpretable dimension-wise reviewer layer and scoped decisions, accounting for evidence incompleteness.
Relevance to SCOPE: Directly addresses open retrieval and special-case evidence; essential prior art.
Verification status: Publisher metadata, abstract, and selected full-text sections checked; interpretation boundary labeled. Bibliographic verification is not exhaustive critical appraisal.

Full title: MultiVerS: Improving scientific claim verification with weak supervision and full-document context
Authors: David Wadden; Kyle Lo; Lucy Lu Wang; Arman Cohan; Iz Beltagy; Hannaneh Hajishirzi
Research problem: Improve scientific verification with document context and limited rationale annotation.
Methodology: Multitask model jointly predicts document labels and sentence rationales; uses heuristic document labels for weak supervision.
Dataset: SciFact, COVIDFact, HealthVer.
Main contribution: Jointly predicts document-level verification labels and rationale sentences using full-document context and weak supervision.
Reported findings / publication output: Reports improvements over two baselines across three datasets, including zero/few-shot domain adaptation.
Documented limitation or task boundary c: Paper full text checked: rationale sentences can omit needed context, including qualifiers and coreference, even when the full document is encoded. This is a rationale/context caveat, not evidence that the model ignores context. See paper discussion of rationale limitations; [ACL paper](https://aclanthology.org/2022.findings-naacl.6/).
Analyst interpretation and potential gap: Conventional support/refute/insufficient labels; does not evaluate a complete exposed scope schema or human-review workflow. Potential gap: Novelty must be compared against MultiVerS; possible contribution is an interpretable scope review layer if experiments establish value.
Relevance to SCOPE: Very close prior art: document context, joint rationale and relation prediction, domain adaptation.
Verification status: Publisher metadata, abstract, and selected full-text sections checked; interpretation boundary labeled. Bibliographic verification is not exhaustive critical appraisal.
